overview: This file brings together a December 1945 diplomatic note and two June 1947 telegrams concerning the disposition and exploitation of raw materials under the Allied occupation of Japan. The first document proposes exporting Japanese stockpiles of rubber, tin, and antimony to earn foreign exchange for essential imports, while preserving inter-Allied consultation through the Far Eastern Advisory Commission and international commodity-allocation bodies. The later telegrams concern the American-operated phosphate project on Angaur Island, undertaken with Japanese labor to supply fertilizer to Japan, and the political dispute created by British and Australian claims that the Allies had not been consulted. Collectively, the documents illuminate the relationship between occupation finance, Japanese subsistence, strategic commodities, and tensions within the Allied coalition.

subfiles.title: Diplomatic note to the Netherlands ambassador on Japanese raw-material stockpiles
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Dr. A. Loudon, Ambassador of the Netherlands
subfiles.about: The Department seeks Dutch agreement to the immediate shipment to the United States of exportable Japanese stocks of rubber, tin, and antimony.
subfiles.summary: SCAP had located Japanese stockpiles of 10,000 tons of rubber, 4,200 tons of tin, and 1,017 tons of antimony, much of which Washington believed could be released through strict conservation and substitution. The United States proposed purchasing the exportable material with dollars so Japan could obtain imports needed for minimum subsistence, subject to possible later reallocation through Allied and international commodity bodies. The note explains that the United States Commercial Company would handle deliveries because direct commercial contact between Japanese and foreign nationals was considered inadvisable. It also anticipates an Inter-Allied Supply Committee to consult on scarce Japanese exports.

subfiles.title: SCAP press statement defending the Angaur phosphate project
subfiles.to: War Department, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: SCAP transmits a press statement defending its use of Angaur phosphate and requests representations to the British government over public criticism.
subfiles.summary: The statement answers a London report that Britain had not been consulted before Japanese personnel were authorized to operate the Angaur phosphate project. SCAP argues that the project had operated for more than a year with Combined Food Board authorization, later under contract to J.H. Pomeroy and Company, and was essential to Japan's fertilizer supply and reduced American occupation costs. It maintains that American control of Angaur and the Far Eastern Commission's jurisdiction over Japan Proper made the British objection misplaced. The telegram characterizes British criticism, possibly linked to dissatisfaction over whaling policy, as harmful to Allied solidarity and asks the Department to consider representations in London.

subfiles.title: Atcheson telegram on Australian objections to the Angaur project
subfiles.to: War Department, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: SCAP recommends a detailed reply to the Australian Embassy and complains that Washington failed to alert Tokyo to Allied objections before the Angaur project proceeded.
subfiles.summary: The telegram proposes telling the Australian Embassy that SCAP had not known of its May 29 aide-mémoire and clarifies that the project used American equipment under continuous SCAP supervision. Japanese personnel were to remain segregated under military-government control and return to Japan when the work ended. Atcheson interprets British criticism as encouraged by Australia and connects it with Australian press criticism of MacArthur's authorization of another Japanese Antarctic whaling expedition. He protests that Washington's failure to transmit the Australian objection before SCAP issued instructions and a press release left headquarters exposed to what it regarded as false criticism.

interest: The file is useful for showing how mineral policy, food production, and occupation financing were treated as parts of the same problem: Japanese exports and island resources were expected to reduce reliance on U.S. appropriations. The Angaur telegrams are especially revealing about jurisdictional ambiguity beyond Japan Proper and about deteriorating relations among occupation partners, including SCAP's unusually blunt internal assessment of British and Australian motives. The first note also documents an early proposal for multilateral machinery to allocate scarce Japanese exports while preventing direct foreign commercial dealings with Japanese nationals.
